t:
(a) 
The Secretary shall, in consultation with the Administrator of the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration, the Administrator of the Maritime Administration, the Administrator of the National Aeronautics and Space Administration, and the Technical Panel established under section 8, prepare a comprehensive technology application and market development plan that will permit realization of the ten-thousand-megawatt national goal by the year 1999. Such plans shall include at a minimum—

        (1) 
an assessment of those Government actions required to achieve a two-hundred-to four-hundred-megawatt electrical-commercial demonstration of ocean thermal energy conversion systems in time to have industry meet the goal contained in section 2(b)(2) including a listing of those financial, property, and patent right packages most likely to lead to early commercial demonstration at minimum cost to the Federal Government;
 
        (2) 
an assessment of further Government actions required to permit expansion of the domestic ocean thermal energy conversion industry to meet the goal contained in section 2(b)(3);
 
        (3) 
an analysis of further Government actions necessary to aid the industry in minimizing and removing any legal and institutional barriers such as the designation of a lead agency; and
 
        (4) 
an assessment of the necessary Government actions to assist in eliminating economic uncertainties through financial incentives, such as loan guarantees, price supports, or other inducements.
  
    (b) The Secretary shall transmit such comprehensive technology application and market development plan to the Congress within three years after the date of enactment of this Act, and update the plan on an annual basis thereafter.
 
    (c) 
As part of the competitive procurement initiative for design and construction of the pilot and demonstration projects authorized in section 10(c), each respondent shall include in its proposal (1) a plan leading to a full-scale, first-of-a-kind facility based on a proposed demonstration system; and (2) the financial and other contributions the respondent will make toward meeting the national goals.

fable.w: The tempting reading is "No": the three named Administrators are all federal officials, and the plan is simply transmitted to Congress, both of which stay inside the government. But the Secretary must also consult the Technical Panel established under section 8, an advisory panel, before preparing a plan that sets out the Government's actions and incentives for commercialization. The section does not state the panel's membership, so treating it as an outside advisory body is an inference, consistent with how advisory boards of unstated membership are treated in the examples. A plan of this kind is closer to a federal policy decision than to a mere study, though that point is debatable.
fable.s: and the Technical Panel established under section 8, prepare a comprehensive technology application and market development plan

opus.w: Besides consulting other federal agencies, which doesn't count, the Secretary must consult the section 8 Technical Panel. As I recall the Act, that is an advisory panel with outside experts from industry and academia, though this section doesn't say so. The plan sets out which government actions to take, so the consultation feeds a federal policy decision rather than just a study or a report to Congress.
opus.s: The Secretary shall, in consultation with the Administrator of the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration, the Administrator of the Maritime Administration, the Administrator of the National Aeronautics and Space Administration, and the Technical Panel established under section 8, prepare a comprehensive technology application and market development plan
opus.b:
I labelled this **Yes**, with moderate confidence (0.62).

1. **The tempting "No" readings.** Most of the consultation in subsection (a) is with other federal agencies: NOAA, the Maritime Administration and NASA. That is coordination inside the government and doesn't count. Subsection (b) is only a report to Congress, which also stays inside the government. Subsection (c) is about procurement proposals, which work like applications. Finally, Example 3 suggests that consulting on a study isn't participation.

2. **Why the label is still "Yes".** The Secretary must also consult the "Technical Panel established under section 8." The section itself doesn't say who sits on that panel. From what I recall of the 1980 Ocean Thermal Energy Conversion Act, it sits under the Energy Research Advisory Board and is made up of people from industry and academia. That is an advisory body with non-federal members. Also, this isn't just a study: the plan sets out which government actions to take, such as financial incentives and naming a lead agency. That makes it a policy decision, which is unlike Example 3. Example 12 also counted recommendations from a committee whose membership wasn't stated.

3. **Why confidence is only moderate.** The panel's non-federal makeup comes from my memory of section 8, not from this text. There is also a fair argument that preparing a plan is closer to the study in Example 3.

Technical Panels in this context are typically composed of outside experts, who are considered outside the federal government. Therefore, this consultation involves an outside party in a federal decision-making process.
